steps.text: Define L=[[I,0],[CA⁻¹,I]], H=[[A,0],[0,S]], and U=[[I,A⁻¹B],[0,I]]. Direct block multiplication gives LH=[[A,0],[C,S]]. Therefore LHU=[[A,B],[C,CA⁻¹B+S]]=M.

If S is invertible, then H⁻¹=[[A⁻¹,0],[0,S⁻¹]]. Both HH⁻¹ and H⁻¹H equal the identity. Thus U⁻¹H⁻¹L⁻¹ is a two-sided inverse of LHU=M.
If M is invertible, then H=L⁻¹MU⁻¹ is invertible, with inverse UM⁻¹L. Write its inverse as [[E,F],[G,J]]. The bottom-right blocks of HH⁻¹=I and H⁻¹H=I give SJ=JS=I. Thus S is invertible.
Multiply U⁻¹H⁻¹ to obtain [[A⁻¹,−A⁻¹BS⁻¹],[0,S⁻¹]]. Its product with L⁻¹ is the displayed inverse. The order of every factor matters. No interchange of matrix factors occurs.

The first block equation is Ax+By=f. Since A is invertible, x=A⁻¹(f−By). Substitute this into Cx+Dy=g to obtain Sy=g−CA⁻¹f. Conversely these two reduced equations imply both original equations. Empty blocks satisfy the same identities.

steps.text: For bounded operators U and V, ‖UVx‖≤‖U‖‖V‖‖x‖. Thus ‖UV‖≤‖U‖‖V‖. Induction gives ‖Tⁿ‖≤qⁿ for n≥1. Also ‖I‖≤1, including the zero space.

Let P_N=∑_{n=0}^N Tⁿ. For m>N, the triangle inequality gives ‖P_m−P_N‖≤∑_{n=N+1}^m qⁿ≤q^(N+1)/(1−q). The linked scalar geometric series proves that this bound tends to 0. Hence the partial sums form a Cauchy sequence in operator norm.

For each x, the sequence P_Nx is Cauchy because ‖(P_m−P_N)x‖≤‖P_m−P_N‖‖x‖. Completeness of E gives a limit Rx. Limits preserve addition and scalar multiplication, so R is linear. The bound ‖P_Nx‖≤(∑_{n=0}^N qⁿ)‖x‖ gives ‖Rx‖≤‖x‖/(1−q). Thus R is bounded.

For every x, take m→∞ in the tail estimate to obtain ‖(R−P_N)x‖≤q^(N+1)‖x‖/(1−q). Continuity of the norm follows from |‖u‖−‖v‖|≤‖u−v‖. The definition of operator norm gives the stated tail bound and proves P_N→R in operator norm.

Finite cancellation gives (I−T)P_N=P_N(I−T)=I−T^(N+1). The operator norm of T^(N+1) is at most q^(N+1), which tends to 0. Products with the fixed bounded operator I−T preserve operator-norm limits by the first-step bound. Therefore (I−T)R=R(I−T)=I.
The tail and inverse bounds also hold when q=0. In that case T=0, R=I, and every tail is 0. The proof does not require different operators to commute. It uses only powers of T.

worked_application.goal: Solve u(x)−(1/2)∫₀ˣu(t)dt=1 for x in [0,1], and bound a finite approximation.
hypotheses: E=C([0,1],ℝ) with the uniform norm is complete.
Define (Tu)(x)=(1/2)∫₀ˣu(t)dt. This operator is linear and maps continuous functions to continuous functions.

Completeness follows directly: a uniform Cauchy sequence has pointwise real limits. The same Cauchy estimate proves uniform convergence. For a point x, select one continuous approximant within ε/3 of the limit. Its continuity and the triangle inequality prove continuity of the limit at x.

steps.text: For ‖u‖∞≤1, |(Tu)(x)|≤x/2≤1/2. The function u=1 attains 1/2 at x=1. Thus ‖T‖=1/2.

  simp only [gaussSum, AddChar.inv_apply, Finset.sum_mul, Finset.mul_sum, MulChar.inv_apply']
  conv =>

steps.text: Every nonzero character value has finite multiplicative order because its source group is finite. Thus |χ(x)|=1 for x≠0 and |ψ(x)|=1 for all x. Their complex conjugates equal their inverses.
Choose a∈F× with χ(a)≠1. The bijection x↦ax on F× shows ∑_{x∈F×}χ(x)=χ(a)∑_{x∈F×}χ(x). Subtract the two sides and divide by 1−χ(a). Therefore the multiplicative character sum is 0.

Choose z∈F with ψ(z)≠1. The bijection x↦x+z gives ∑_{x∈F}ψ(x)=ψ(z)∑_{x∈F}ψ(x), so this additive character sum is 0. If b≠0, multiplication by b permutes F. Hence ∑_{y∈F}ψ(by)=0. Remove the y=0 term to obtain ∑_{y∈F×}ψ(by)=−1. For b=0 the latter sum is q−1.

Expand |G|²=G conjugate(G) as a finite double sum. Terms with x=0 or y=0 vanish. For each y≠0, write x=ty. This bijection changes χ(x)conjugate(χ(y)) to χ(t), and ψ(x)conjugate(ψ(y)) to ψ((t−1)y). Thus |G|²=∑_{t∈F×}χ(t)∑_{y∈F×}ψ((t−1)y).
Separate t=1. Its inner sum is q−1 and χ(1)=1. Every other t contributes −χ(t). The zero sum in step 2 gives ∑_{t≠0,1}χ(t)=−1. Therefore |G|²=(q−1)−(−1)=q.

If χ²=1 on F×, all its values are real and equal to 1 or −1. Therefore conjugate(G)=∑χ(x)ψ(−x). Replace x by −x to obtain conjugate(G)=χ(−1)G. Since χ(−1)²=1, the magnitude equation yields χ(−1)G²=q, or G²=χ(−1)q.

worked_application.goal: Compute ∑_{x=0}^4 exp(2πiax²/5) for a=1 and a=2.
hypotheses: F=ℤ/5ℤ is a field. Put ζ=exp(2πi/5) and ψ(t)=ζᵗ.

The squares x² for x=0,1,2,3,4 are 0,1,4,4,1. Thus the number of roots of x²=t is 1+χ(t) for each t in F. For a≠0, the additive-character sum ∑_tψ(at) is 0. Therefore S(a)=∑_tχ(t)ψ(at).

lemma LocalizedModule.map_exact (g : M₀ →ₗ[R] M₁) (h : M₁ →ₗ[R] M₂) (ex : Exact g h) :
    Exact (map S (mkLinearMap S M₀) (mkLinearMap S M₁) g)
    (map S (mkLinearMap S M₁) (mkLinearMap S M₂) h) :=
  fun y ↦ Iff.intro
    (induction_on
      (fun m s hy ↦ by
        rw [map_LocalizedModules, ← zero_mk 1, mk_eq, one_smul, smul_zero] at hy
        obtain ⟨a, aS, ha⟩ := Subtype.exists.1 hy
        rw [smul_zero, mk_smul, ← map_smul, ex (a • m)] at ha
        rcases ha with ⟨x, hx⟩
        use mk x (⟨a, aS⟩ * s)
        rw [map_LocalizedModules, hx, ← mk_cancel_common_left ⟨a, aS⟩ s m, mk_smul])
      y)
    fun ⟨x, hx⟩ ↦ by
      revert hx
      refine induction_on (fun m s hx ↦ ?_) x
      rw [← hx, map_LocalizedModules, map_LocalizedModules, (ex (g m)).2 ⟨m, rfl⟩, zero_mk]

steps.text: The induced map is well-defined. If u(tm−sn)=0, linearity gives u(tf(m)−sf(n))=0. The same u proves equality of the image fractions. Composition commutes with localization by evaluation on every fraction.
Since gf=0, the image of S⁻¹f lies in the kernel of S⁻¹g. Conversely let n/s satisfy g(n)/s=0. The definition of equality of fractions gives u∈S with ug(n)=0. Thus g(un)=0.

worked_application.goal: Localize 0→ℤ→ℤ→ℤ/6ℤ→0, whose first nonzero map is multiplication by 6, at powers of 2.
hypotheses: R=ℤ and S={2ⁿ:n≥0}. Multiplication by 6 is injective, and its image is the kernel of reduction modulo 6.

The class of 3 in ℤ/6ℤ disappears because 2·3=0. The class of 2 remains nonzero and has order 3. If all nonzero integers are inverted instead, multiplication by 6 is invertible and the quotient becomes 0.

steps.text: The determinant for n=0 is 1, which agrees with the empty product. For n=1 it is also 1. Assume the formula for n−1 and first take distinct nodes a₀,…,aₙ₋₂.

Replace the last node by an indeterminate X. Expand the determinant along its last row. This gives a polynomial D(X) of degree at most n−1. Its leading coefficient is the determinant of the first n−1 nodes, because the last cofactor has positive sign.
For X=aᵢ with i<n−1, two rows are equal and D(aᵢ)=0. This equality follows from the determinant definition: interchange those rows in each permutation term and pair terms with opposite signs.

For any polynomial P, the identity Xᵏ−aᵏ=(X−a)∑_{j=0}^{k−1}Xᵏ⁻¹⁻ʲaʲ shows P(X)−P(a) is divisible by X−a. Therefore each distinct root aᵢ gives a factor X−aᵢ. After division by earlier factors, evaluation at a later root still gives 0, since the earlier factors are nonzero there.

Thus D(X) is its leading coefficient times ∏_{i<n−1}(X−aᵢ). The induction hypothesis supplies that coefficient. Substitute X=aₙ₋₁ to obtain the full product. If the first n−1 nodes are not distinct, V has repeated rows, and both sides are 0.

If det(V)≠0, its adjugate gives the inverse V⁻¹=adj(V)/det(V). The adjugate identity follows by cofactor expansion: diagonal entries give det(V), and off-diagonal entries give determinants with a repeated row. If det(V)=0, the nodes repeat and V has two equal rows, so V cannot map onto every data vector. The interpolation equations are Vc=y. Thus distinct nodes give exactly one coefficient vector c.

steps.text: The matrix A*A is Hermitian because (A*A)*=A*A. It is positive semidefinite because v*A*Av=‖Av‖²≥0. The linked spectral theorem gives an orthonormal basis vᵢ of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues λᵢ≥0.
Order the positive eigenvalues first, and set σᵢ=√λᵢ. For λᵢ>0 define uᵢ=Avᵢ/σᵢ. Then ⟨uᵢ,uⱼ⟩=⟨vᵢ,A*Avⱼ⟩/(σᵢσⱼ)=λⱼδᵢⱼ/(σᵢσⱼ)=δᵢⱼ. Thus these uᵢ are orthonormal.

If λᵢ=0, then ‖Avᵢ‖²=λᵢ‖vᵢ‖²=0, so Avᵢ=0. Expansion in the vᵢ basis shows that the range of A is exactly the span of the positive-eigenvalue uᵢ. Its dimension is the number of those eigenvalues, namely r.

Extend the r orthonormal vectors uᵢ to an orthonormal basis of ℂᵐ. If their span is proper, choose a vector outside it. Subtract its orthogonal projections onto the existing vectors. The remainder is nonzero and orthogonal to them. Normalize it, and repeat until m vectors exist.
Let U and V have these basis vectors as columns. They are unitary. The equations Avᵢ=σᵢuᵢ for i≤r and Avᵢ=0 otherwise show U*AV=Σ. Multiply by U and V* to obtain A=UΣV*.
For x=∑cᵢvᵢ, orthonormality gives ‖Ax‖²=∑_{i≤r}σᵢ²|cᵢ|²≤σ₁²‖x‖². Equality holds for x=v₁ if r>0. If r=0, A=0. This proves the operator norm formula.

steps.text: Compute A*A=[[1,1],[1,2]]. Its characteristic polynomial is λ²−3λ+1. The eigenvalues are λ±=(3±√5)/2, both positive.

The two left singular vectors span the first 2 coordinate directions. Add (0,0,1) to obtain U. These vectors and the vλ give A=UΣV*. The largest amplification is φ, and the smallest amplification on the domain is φ⁻¹.

The Euclidean condition number for this full-column-rank map is their ratio φ²=(3+√5)/2. The determinant of its top 2×2 block is 1, but this does not force equal amplification in different directions.

steps.text: For a>0, t^(a−1) is integrable on (0,1), with integral 1/a. For t≥1, t^(a−1)e^(−t)≤Ce^(−t/2) for some finite C. If a≤1, take C=1. If a>1, differentiation shows t^(a−1)e^(−t/2) has a finite maximum. Hence Γ(a) is finite. The same proof applies to Γ(b) and Γ(a+b).

The Beta integrand is integrable near 0 because a>0 and (1−s)^(b−1) is bounded on (0,1/2). It is integrable near 1 because b>0 and s^(a−1) is bounded on (1/2,1). Thus B(a,b) is finite. Γ(a+b)>0 because its integrand is positive on (1,2).
Tonelli gives Γ(a)Γ(b)=∫_{(0,∞)²}u^(a−1)v^(b−1)e^(−u−v)dudv. The integrand is nonnegative, so the factorization is valid.

Use u=rs and v=r(1−s), with r>0 and 0<s<1. The inverse map is r=u+v and s=u/(u+v), so this is a smooth bijection. Its absolute Jacobian is r. The change-of-variables formula gives the integrand r^(a+b−1)e^(−r)s^(a−1)(1−s)^(b−1).
Tonelli factors the transformed integral into Γ(a+b)B(a,b). Divide by the positive Γ(a+b) to obtain the ratio formula.

For the second identity, set s=x/(1+x). Then x=s/(1−s) and dx=ds/(1−s)². Direct substitution gives x^(a−1)(1+x)^(−a−b)dx=s^(a−1)(1−s)^(b−1)ds. The change-of-variables formula and the convergence already proved give the result.

steps.text: Induction on n shows Hₙ is monic of degree n. The term xHₙ has degree n+1 and leading coefficient 1. The derivative Hₙ′ has smaller degree, so subtraction cannot change that leading term.
Put φ(x)=e^(−x²/2). Since φ′=−xφ, induction and the product rule give φ^(n)=(-1)ⁿHₙφ. The induction step is D((-1)ⁿHₙφ)=(-1)ⁿ(Hₙ′−xHₙ)φ=(-1)ⁿ⁺¹Hₙ₊₁φ.

Every polynomial times φ is integrable, and tends to 0 at ±∞. For each integer k≥0, |x|ᵏe^(−x²/2) has a finite integral. For large |x|, k log|x|≤x²/4, so the expression is at most e^(−x²/4). The linked Gaussian integral proves that bound is integrable. This also proves the boundary limit.

On each finite interval, integrate Hₘφ^(n) by parts n times. Then send both endpoints to infinity. Every boundary term is a polynomial times φ, so step 3 makes it vanish. Absolute integrability permits the improper limits. The two factors (-1)ⁿ cancel, giving ∫HₘHₙφ=∫Hₘ^(n)φ.
If n>m, the nth derivative of Hₘ is 0, so the integral is 0. If n=m, monicity gives Hₙ^(n)=n!, and the linked Gaussian integral gives n!√(2π).
If n<m, interchange m and n in the integral and use the n>m case. Multiplication of the real polynomial values is commutative. This covers every pair of indices, including m=n=0.

worked_application.title: A Gaussian control variate from orthogonal polynomials
worked_application.goal: Find the best approximation of X⁴ by a+b(X²−1) in mean square, for a standard normal variable X.
hypotheses: The density of X is e^(−x²/2)/√(2π). Its normalization follows from the Gaussian integral.
Mean-square error is the Gaussian polynomial inner product of the residual with itself.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Hermite orthogonality makes the least-squares coefficients independent. It also computes the residual variance exactly.

steps.text: The recurrence gives H₂=x²−1 and H₄=x⁴−6x²+3. Therefore x⁴=H₄+6H₂+3H₀.
The residual is H₄+(6−b)H₂+(3−a)H₀. Orthogonality gives its squared norm 4!+2!(6−b)²+(3−a)²=24+2(6−b)²+(3−a)².
This expression has its unique minimum at a=3 and b=6. The best approximation is 3+6(X²−1), and its mean-square error is 24.
Orthogonality with H₀ gives E[X⁴]=3. The squared norm of X⁴ is 24+36·2+9=105. Thus Var(X⁴)=105−9=96.
The adjusted estimator X⁴−6(X²−1) still has mean 3 because E[H₂]=0. Its centered residual is H₄, so its variance is 24. The orthogonal calculation reduces the variance from 96 to 24.

worked_application.result: The best coefficients are a=3 and b=6. The residual variance is 24.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: Different Hermite conventions use different Gaussian weights and normalization constants.
The polynomial projection is in Gaussian L². It does not minimize the uniform error on ℝ.

results.name: Riesz representation theorem for Hilbert spaces
results.statement: Let H be a Hilbert space and φ:H→ℂ a bounded linear functional with ‖φ‖=sup|φ(x)|/‖x‖. Then there exists a unique y∈H such that φ(x)=⟨x,y⟩ for all x∈H, and ‖φ‖=‖y‖.
hypotheses: H is complete for its inner product norm. φ is linear and bounded.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof relies on completeness and the inner product. Uniqueness follows from density of a linear functional's zero set.

definitions.name: bounded linear functional
definitions.text: φ is bounded if ‖φ‖=sup_{x≠0} |φ(x)|/‖x‖ < ∞.

results.proof_status: authored proof; no local formal verification

proof.verification: Authored proof. No local formal verification.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: If φ=0, set y=0. Otherwise, kerφ={x: φ(x)=0} is a proper closed subspace.
Take z∈H∖kerφ. Then kerφ and span{z} are orthogonal complements (up to scaling) because H=kerφ⊕span{z}.
For each x∈H, write x=u+tv where u∈kerφ and v∈span{z}. Then φ(x)=tφ(v).
Set y=(φ(v)/‖v‖²)v. Then ⟨x,y⟩=⟨u,y⟩+t⟨v,y⟩=t(φ(v)/‖v‖²)‖v‖²=tφ(v)=φ(x).
Uniqueness: if ⟨x,y₁⟩=⟨x,y₂⟩ for all x, then ⟨x,y₁−y₂⟩=0, so y₁=y₂.

worked_application.title: Recovering a test function from moment data
worked_application.goal: Given moments mₙ=∫₀¹ tⁿg(t)dt for n=0,1,…,5 with g∈L²[0,1], recover g.
hypotheses: g∈L²[0,1] and the moments m₀,...,m₅ are given. Assume m₀=1/2, m₁=1/3, m₂=1/4, m₃=1/5, m₄=1/6, m₅=1/7.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Each moment defines a linear functional on L². Riesz representation says each moment comes from an inner product with a unique test function.

steps.text: Define φ(g)=mₙ. By Riesz, φ corresponds to fₙ(t)=tⁿ in L².
The inner product ⟨g,tⁿ⟩=∫₀¹ g(t)tⁿdt=mₙ. Each moment recovers the projection of g onto fₙ.
Expand g in the orthonormal basis {√2sin(πkt), k=1,2,...}. Compute ⟨g,sin(πkt)⟩ from the moments.
With 6 moments, approximate g by the first few basis terms. Least-squares fit ∑ᵢ₌₁³ cᵢ√2sin(πit) satisfies the moment equations.

worked_application.result: g is uniquely determined by its moments; truncation gives an L² approximation.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: Complex-valued functionals require complex Hilbert spaces. Real functionals give real y.
A non-complete inner product space lacks this representation.

results.name: Closed range theorem for Banach spaces
results.statement: Let X,Y be Banach spaces and T:X→Y a bounded linear operator. Then T has closed range if and only if T* has closed range, and if and only if ∃c>0 such that dist(x,kerT)≤c‖Tx‖ for all x∈X.
hypotheses: X and Y are Banach spaces. T is linear and bounded.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof uses the open mapping theorem and duality. Closed range is equivalent to a uniform lower bound on the quotient map.

definitions.name: closed range
definitions.text: T has closed range if imT is closed in Y.

definitions.name: distance to kernel
definitions.text: dist(x,kerT)=inf{‖x−y‖: y∈kerT}.

results.proof_status: authored proof; no local formal verification

proof.verification: Authored proof. No local formal verification.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: If T has closed range, then X/kerT ≅ imT. The quotient map is an isomorphism onto its range.
By the open mapping theorem, the inverse is also bounded: ∃c>0 with ‖x̄‖≤c‖Tx‖ for quotient norms.
The quotient norm satisfies ‖x̄‖=inf{‖x−y‖: y∈kerT}=dist(x,kerT).
Conversely, the lower bound dist(x,kerT)≤c‖Tx‖ implies imT is closed: if Txₙ→z, then kerT is contained in the closure of {xₙ}, forcing the sequence to have a limit.
Apply duality: T has closed range ⟺ (imT)* surjects onto imT*=kerT* ⟺ T* has closed range.

worked_application.title: Invertibility of a Fredholm operator via closed range
worked_application.goal: Determine when I+K is invertible for a compact operator K on ℓ².
hypotheses: K is compact on ℓ². The operator I+K is Fredholm with index 0.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: A Fredholm operator is invertible iff its kernel is trivial. Closed range shows this is equivalent to a lower bound on ‖(I+K)x‖.

steps.text: If (I+K)x=0, then x=−Kx. Since K is compact, kerK={0} forces x=0. So ker(I+K)={0}.
Apply closed range: imI+K is closed iff ∃c>0 with ‖x‖≤c‖(I+K)x‖. By compactness of K, this holds.
Since dim(kerI+K)=0 and I+K has closed range, I+K is surjective (by Fredholm index).
Therefore I+K is bijective and its inverse is bounded by the closed range theorem.

worked_application.result: I+K is invertible on ℓ² when K is compact.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The theorem requires Banach spaces; Hilbert spaces give a simpler self-adjoint picture.
Non-closed ranges occur for operators like differentiation on L² without suitable domain restrictions.

results.name: Arzelà-Ascoli compactness criterion
results.statement: Let K be a compact metric space and C(K) the space of continuous functions K→ℝ with the uniform norm ‖f‖=max|f(x)|. A subset F⊆C(K) is compact if and only if F is closed, bounded, and equicontinuous: ∀ε>0 ∃δ>0 such that d(x,y)<δ implies |f(x)−f(y)|<ε for all f∈F.
hypotheses: K is compact. C(K) is the Banach space with uniform norm.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof relies on compactness of K and the metric structure. Diagonalization picks a convergent subsequence.

definitions.name: equicontinuous
definitions.text: F is equicontinuous if all members have the same modulus of continuity uniformly.

results.proof_status: authored proof; no local formal verification

proof.verification: Authored proof. No local formal verification.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: If F is compact, it is closed and bounded. For equicontinuity, each f∈F is uniformly continuous on K.
Given ε>0, for each f∈F find δf such that d(x,y)<δf implies |f(x)−f(y)|<ε/3. Choose the minimum over a finite subcover.
Conversely, assume F is closed, bounded, equicontinuous. Pick a dense sequence {xₙ} in K. Use diagonal diagonalization to extract a convergent subsequence along {xₙ}.
For any x∈K, by equicontinuity and density, the limit of the subsequence at x exists. Let f(x)=this limit.
By equicontinuity and boundedness, f is continuous and ‖f‖≤supf. Thus f∈F and F contains the limit, proving F is compact.

worked_application.title: Compactness of integral operator range
worked_application.goal: Show that {(Tf)(x)=∫₀¹ K(x,y)f(y)dy: ‖f‖₁≤1} is compact in C[0,1].
hypotheses: K is continuous on [0,1]². The operator T:L¹[0,1]→C[0,1] is defined by (Tf)(x)=∫₀¹ K(x,y)f(y)dy.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Arzelà-Ascoli shows this image is compact by verifying boundedness and equicontinuity.

steps.text: Boundedness: ‖Tf‖∞≤max|K|·∫|f|=max|K|·‖f‖₁≤max|K|.
Equicontinuity: |Tf(x)−Tf(y)|≤∫₀¹ |K(x,t)−K(y,t)|·|f(t)|dt≤‖f‖₁·max_t supsₓ,ᵧ |K(x,t)−K(y,t)|.
Since K is uniformly continuous on the compact set [0,1]², for each ε>0 there exists δ such that |x−y|<δ implies max_t |K(x,t)−K(y,t)|<ε.
Therefore |Tf(x)−Tf(y)|<ε for all ‖f‖₁≤1 when |x−y|<δ. The set {Tf: ‖f‖₁≤1} is equicontinuous and bounded.

worked_application.result: {Tf: ‖f‖₁≤1} is compact in C[0,1].
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: Equicontinuity is essential; dropping it allows non-compact subsets (e.g., Dirac masses).
Arzelà-Ascoli is for sequences; sequential compactness equals compactness in metric spaces.

results.name: Radon-Nikodym decomposition and derivative
results.statement: Let (X,Σ,μ) be a σ-finite measure space and ν a σ-finite signed measure on the same space. Then ν admits a unique decomposition ν=νₐ+νₛ where νₐ is absolutely continuous with respect to μ and νₛ is singular with respect to μ (supported on a μ-null set). If νₐ≪μ, then ∃g∈L¹(μ) such that νₐ(E)=∫ₑ g dμ for all E∈Σ. The function g is the Radon-Nikodym derivative dνₐ/dμ.
hypotheses: (X,Σ,μ) is a σ-finite measure space. ν is a σ-finite signed measure.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof uses monotone class arguments and completeness of L². Lebesgue decomposition is first shown.

definitions.name: absolutely continuous
definitions.text: ν≪μ if μ(E)=0 implies ν(E)=0 for all E∈Σ.

definitions.name: singular measures
definitions.text: ν⊥μ if there exists E with μ(Eᶜ)=0 and ν(E)=0.

results.proof_status: authored proof; no local formal verification

proof.verification: Authored proof. No local formal verification.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Consider the decomposition X=A∪B with A,B disjoint, ν(A)≥0, ν(B)≤0 (Hahn decomposition of signed ν).
Define νₐ(E)=ν(E∩A)−ν(E∩B)⁻ and νₛ(E)=ν(E∩B)⁺. Then ν=νₐ+νₛ with νₐ=|νₐ|≤|ν|.
νₛ is supported on a μ-null set if ν⊥μ. To show: find E with μ(Eᶜ)=0 and νₛ(E)=0.
If νₐ≪μ, consider μ+|νₐ| to get Radon-Nikodym: dνₐ/d(μ+|νₐ|) exists. Multiply by the Radon-Nikodym derivative of μ w.r.t. μ+|νₐ| to get g.
Uniqueness of g: if νₐ(E)=∫ₑ g dμ=∫ₑ h dμ for all E, then ∫(g−h)χₑ dμ=0, so g=h μ-a.e.

worked_application.title: Decomposing a measure into singular and absolutely continuous parts
worked_application.goal: Decompose the measure ν on [0,1] given by ν(E)=∫ₑ cos(2πx)dx + δ₁/₂(E).
hypotheses: ν has two parts: an absolutely continuous part (integral of cosine) and a singular Dirac mass at 1/2.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Radon-Nikodym decomposes ν=νₐ+νₛ where νₐ has density g and νₛ is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure.

steps.text: Define νₐ(E)=∫ₑ cos(2πx)dx. Then dνₐ/dμ=cos(2πx), which is in L¹[0,1].
Define νₛ(E)=δ₁/₂(E)=1 if 1/2∈E, 0 otherwise. This is supported on the singleton {1/2}.
The set {1/2} has Lebesgue measure zero. Therefore νₛ(E)=0 whenever E is open or contains no {1/2}.
Verify: ν(E)=νₐ(E)+νₛ(E)=∫ₑ cos(2πx)dx + 1 if E⊇{1/2}, 0 if 1/2∉E.

worked_application.result: νₐ has density g=cos(2πx) and νₛ=δ₁/₂; the decomposition ν=νₐ+νₛ is unique.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: For complex measures, use the polar decomposition first to reduce to positive measures.
σ-finiteness is essential; failure gives non-measurable singular parts.

results.name: Hahn-Banach hyperplane separation theorem
results.statement: Let X be a locally convex Hausdorff topological vector space and A,B nonempty disjoint convex subsets with A open. Then there exists a continuous linear functional f:X→ℝ and α∈ℝ such that f(a)<α≤f(b) for all a∈A,b∈B.
hypotheses: X is a locally convex Hausdorff space. A and B are convex and disjoint.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: Fundamental result.

definitions.name: locally convex
definitions.text: Every point has a basis of convex neighborhoods.

results.proof_status: authored

proof.verification: Authored. No formal check.
proof.scope: Full statement.

steps.text: By the geometric Hahn-Banach, A and B can be separated by a hyperplane. Existence follows from openness of A.
Let C=A−B={a−b: a∈A,b∈B}. This is open and convex with 0∉C (since A∩B=∅).
Find a closed hyperplane containing C in its positive half-space. Continuity of f follows from openness of C.

worked_application.goal: Separate A={x∈ℝ²: ‖x‖≤1} from B={x∈ℝ²: x·(1,0)>2}.
hypotheses: A is the closed unit disk; B is open half-space to the right.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Hahn-Banach gives f with f(a)≤α<f(b) for all a∈A,b∈B.

steps.text: Choose f(x,y)=x. Then f(A)⊆[−1,1] and f(B)⊆(2,∞).
Set α=1. Then f(a)≤1<2≤f(b) for all a∈A,b∈B.
The hyperplane {x=1} separates them: disk touches it at (1,0); half-space lies beyond.

worked_application.verification: Geometric verification.

Openness is essential; closed A and B can be disjoint but inseparable.

results.name: Brouwer fixed-point theorem
results.statement: Every continuous map f:D→D of a convex compact subset D of ℝⁿ into itself has a fixed point: ∃x∈D with f(x)=x.
hypotheses: D is convex and compact in ℝⁿ. f:D→D is continuous.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: Fundamental result.

definitions.name: fixed point
definitions.text: A point x where f(x)=x.

results.proof_status: authored

proof.verification: Authored. No formal check.
proof.scope: Full statement.

steps.text: Suppose f has no fixed point. Then g(x)=f(x)−x never vanishes. Define h(x)=x−tg(x)/‖g(x)‖ for t>0 small.
For t small, h:D→D and h is homotopic to the identity via F(x,s)=x−sg(x)/‖g(x)‖ rel ∂D.
The topological degree of id is 1 (by definition). The degree of h is also 1 (homotopy invariance).
But if f(x)≠x for all x, then h can retract D to its boundary, making degree=0. Contradiction.

worked_application.title: Fixed point of a gradient flow on a disk
worked_application.goal: Show f(x,y)=((x+y)/2, (x−y)/2) has a fixed point on D={(x,y): x²+y²≤1}.
hypotheses: f is continuous and f(D)⊆D (check: ‖f(x,y)‖²=((x+y)²+(x−y)²)/4=(x²+y²)/2≤1/2<1).
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: f maps the closed disk to itself continuously, so Brouwer guarantees a fixed point.

steps.text: Solve f(x,y)=(x,y): (x+y)/2=x and (x−y)/2=y. Simplify: y/2=x and x/2=y.
From y=2x and x=2y: y=2(2y)=4y, so 3y=0 and y=0. Thus x=0.

worked_application.result: (0,0) is the unique fixed point of f on D.
worked_application.verification: Direct verification.

limitations: The theorem requires compactness; f:[0,∞)→[0,∞) with f(x)=x+1 is fixed-point-free.
The dimension matters: fails in infinite dimensions (e.g., f:ℓ²→ℓ² with f(x)=x/2+e₁ has no fixed point).

results.name: Lovász Local Lemma for independent events
results.statement: Let A₁,...,Aₙ be events in a probability space with P(Aᵢ)≤p. If each event is independent of all but at most d others, and ep(d+1)≤1, then P(⋂ᵢ Āᵢ)>0. Thus there exists an outcome where none of the events occur.
hypotheses: P(Aᵢ)≤p for all i. Each Aᵢ is independent of all but at most d of the other events.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: Fundamental result.

definitions.name: independent events
definitions.text: Aᵢ is independent of a set S if P(Aᵢ|∩_{j∈S}Aⱼ)=P(Aᵢ).

results.proof_status: authored

proof.verification: Authored. No formal check.
proof.scope: Full statement.

steps.text: Define xᵢ=p for each i. The condition ep(d+1)≤1 ensures xᵢ≤1/(e(d+1)).
By induction on a permutation, show P(Aᵢ|F)≤xᵢ where F is any event in the σ-algebra generated by dependent events.
The probability P(⋂Āᵢ)=∏(1−P(Aᵢ|Fᵢ))≥∏(1−xᵢ)≥(1−p)ⁿ>0 when ep(d+1)<1.

worked_application.title: Proper coloring with few colors via the lemma
worked_application.goal: Show that every graph with degree ≤Δ has a proper 2-coloring with probability >0 if Δ is bounded.
hypotheses: Graph G has n vertices, each with degree ≤Δ. Color each vertex red/blue independently with probability 1/2.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Let Aᵢ be the event that edge i is monochromatic. Then P(Aᵢ)=1/2 and each Aᵢ depends on at most 2Δ other edges.

steps.text: For monochromatic event: P(both endpoints same color)=1/2.
Each edge depends on edges sharing its endpoints: at most 2Δ−2 other edges in a Δ-regular graph.
For small Δ, this works. For Δ≥2, use weighted version or multiple rounds to color with O(Δ) colors.

worked_application.verification: Probabilistic argument.

The bound ep(d+1)≤1 is tight up to constants; the lemma fails if ep(d+1)>e.

results.name: Spectral theorem for bounded self-adjoint operators
results.statement: Let H be a Hilbert space and T:H→H a bounded self-adjoint operator. Then there exists a unique spectral measure E on ℝ such that T=∫λ dE(λ). For every bounded Borel measurable f:ℝ→ℝ, f(T)=∫f(λ)dE(λ) is well-defined bounded self-adjoint operator.
hypotheses: H is complete. T is bounded and self-adjoint (T*=T).
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: Fundamental result using Hilbert space structure and spectrum definition.

definitions.name: spectral measure
definitions.text: E is a spectral measure if E(∅)=0, E(ℝ)=I, E(A∩B)=E(A)E(B), and E(A∪B)=E(A)+E(B)−E(A∩B).

definitions.name: functional calculus
definitions.text: For f Borel measurable, f(T)=∫f(λ)dE(λ) defines an operator with σ(f(T))=f(σ(T)).

results.proof_status: authored

proof.verification: Authored. No formal check.
proof.scope: Full statement.

steps.text: For bounded T, σ(T)⊆[−‖T‖,‖T‖]. The resolvent (T−zI)⁻¹ is analytic off σ(T).
By Riesz representation, for each x,y∈H the function f(z)=⟨(T−zI)⁻¹x,y⟩ has a representing measure μₓ,ᵧ on σ(T).
Define E(A)=the projection operator such that ⟨E(A)x,y⟩=μₓ,ᵧ(A) for Borel A⊆σ(T).
Verify E is a spectral measure: projection-valued and additive. Then T=∫λdE(λ) by the functional calculus.
Uniqueness: if T=∫λdE'(λ), then for all bounded Borel f, ∫f dE'=f(T)=∫f dE, so E'=E.

results.name: Lax-Milgram variational lemma
results.statement: Let H be a Hilbert space and a:H×H→ℝ a bilinear form that is continuous (∃M: |a(u,v)|≤M‖u‖‖v‖) and coercive (∃c>0: a(u,u)≥c‖u‖²). For any bounded linear functional φ:H→ℝ, there exists unique u∈H such that a(u,v)=φ(v) for all v∈H.
hypotheses: H is a Hilbert space. a is continuous and coercive. φ is bounded linear.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: Fundamental result using Riesz and Cauchy-Schwarz.

definitions.name: coercive bilinear form
definitions.text: a is coercive if a(u,u)≥c‖u‖² for some c>0 and all u.

definitions.name: variational form
definitions.text: Finding u with a(u,v)=φ(v) for all v is the weak form of a PDE.

results.proof_status: authored

proof.verification: Authored.
proof.scope: Full statement.

steps.text: By Riesz, φ(v)=⟨f,v⟩ for unique f∈H. Define T:H→H by ⟨Tu,v⟩=a(u,v).
By continuity and coercivity: ‖Tu‖≤M‖u‖ and c‖u‖²≤⟨Tu,u⟩≤‖Tu‖·‖u‖, so c‖u‖≤‖Tu‖.
T is bounded below: ‖Tu‖≥c‖u‖. Thus T is injective and imT is closed.
For v⊥imT: ⟨Tv,w⟩=a(v,w)=0 for all w. Set w=v: c‖v‖²≤a(v,v)=0, so v=0. Thus imT=H.
T is bijective and bounded below, so T⁻¹ is bounded. Solve Tu=f: u=T⁻¹f is unique.

worked_application.title: Poisson equation −Δu=f on (0,1) with Dirichlet boundary conditions
worked_application.goal: Show that for every f∈L²(0,1), there exists unique u∈H₀¹(0,1) with ∫₀¹ u'v'=∫₀¹ fv for all v∈H₀¹.
hypotheses: f∈L²(0,1). H₀¹ is the Sobolev space with zero boundary values.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Lax-Milgram applies to a(u,v)=∫u'v' and φ(v)=∫fv on H=H₀¹.

steps.text: Verify coercivity: a(u,u)=∫(u')²=‖u‖²_{H¹}≥c‖u‖²_{L²} by Poincaré.
Verify continuity: |a(u,v)|≤‖u'‖_{L²}·‖v'‖_{L²}≤‖u‖_{H¹}·‖v‖_{H¹}.
Continuity of φ: |φ(v)|=|∫fv|≤‖f‖_{L²}·‖v‖_{L²}≤‖f‖_{L²}·‖v‖_{H¹}.
By Lax-Milgram, ∃unique u∈H₀¹ solving the weak form. Classical solution if f is smooth.

worked_application.result: Unique weak solution u∈H₀¹(0,1) exists; satisfies −u''=f in the distributional sense.
worked_application.verification: Variational formulation verified.

limitations: Requires coercivity; some problems use Fredholm alternative instead.
Boundary conditions must be incorporated into the Hilbert space structure.

results.name: Open mapping theorem for Banach spaces
results.statement: Let X,Y be Banach spaces and T:X→Y a bounded linear operator that is surjective. Then T is an open map: the image of every open set in X is open in Y. Equivalently, ∃c>0 such that for every y∈Y with ‖y‖≤1, there exists x∈X with Tx=y and ‖x‖≤c.
hypotheses: X,Y are Banach spaces. T:X→Y is bounded and surjective.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: Fundamental result using Baire category theorem.

definitions.name: open map
definitions.text: T is open if T(U) is open in Y whenever U is open in X.

definitions.name: surjective
definitions.text: T is surjective (onto) if imT=Y.

results.proof_status: authored

proof.verification: Authored.
proof.scope: Full statement.

steps.text: Since T is surjective and continuous, Y=⋃_n T(B_n) where B_n={x: ‖x‖≤n}.
By Baire category, some B_n has T(B_n) with nonempty interior. Thus T(B₁) has nonempty interior.
Scaling: T(B_r) has interior for r>0. Thus ∃c>0, ε>0: {y: ‖y‖<ε}⊆T({x: ‖x‖<c}).
Every y with ‖y‖=1 lies in some open ball around T(x₀). Thus T is open: T(U)⊇{y: dist(y,T(U))>δ} for U open.

worked_application.title: Inverse of a bijective bounded operator is bounded
worked_application.goal: Show that if T:ℓ²→ℓ² is bounded, bijective, and T⁻¹ exists, then T⁻¹ is bounded.
hypotheses: T:ℓ²→ℓ² is bounded, linear, and bijective.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: T is surjective (bijective); open mapping theorem gives c>0 with ‖x‖≤c‖Tx‖.

steps.text: By open mapping, ∃c with ‖x‖≤c‖Tx‖ for all x∈ℓ².
Let y∈ℓ². Write y=Tx for unique x. Then ‖x‖=‖T⁻¹y‖≤c‖Tx‖=c‖y‖.
Therefore ‖T⁻¹y‖≤c‖y‖ for all y. Thus T⁻¹ is bounded with ‖T⁻¹‖≤c.

worked_application.result: T⁻¹:ℓ²→ℓ² is bounded whenever T is.
worked_application.verification: Direct from open mapping.

limitations: Fails for non-complete spaces; need Banach completeness for Baire category.
Surjectivity is essential; non-surjective operators need not have open images.

results.name: Stone-Weierstrass polynomial approximation theorem
results.statement: Let K be a compact metric space and C(K) the Banach space of continuous real functions with sup norm. Let A⊆C(K) be a subalgebra containing constants and separating points (for x≠y in K, ∃f∈A with f(x)≠f(y)). Then A is dense in C(K).
hypotheses: K is compact. A is a subalgebra of C(K) containing 1 and separating points.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: Fundamental result using the Stone-Weierstrass approximation lemma.

definitions.name: separating points
definitions.text: A separates points if for every x≠y, ∃f∈A with f(x)≠f(y).

definitions.name: subalgebra
definitions.text: A is a subalgebra if it's closed under addition, multiplication, and scalar multiplication.

results.proof_status: authored

proof.verification: Authored.
proof.scope: Full statement.

steps.text: First, A is closed under max and min: for f,g∈A, max(f,g)=f+(g−f)⁺ and |(g−f)⁺|²=(g−f)⁺·(g−f)⁺.
By separating points, for every x≠y and α,β∈ℝ, find f∈A with f(x)=α, f(y)=β.
Given g∈C(K), cover K by neighborhoods Uₓ where g is close to g(x). On each Uₓ, find fₓ∈A with fₓ(x)=g(x).
The function h=max_x(fₓ) is the max of finitely many A-elements (on compact K). Thus h∈A and h≈g.
Iterating, obtain a sequence in A converging uniformly to g. Thus A is dense in C(K).

worked_application.title: Approximating continuous functions by polynomials on [0,1]
worked_application.goal: Show that every continuous f:[0,1]→ℝ can be uniformly approximated by polynomials.
hypotheses: f∈C[0,1]. Want: ∀ε>0, ∃ polynomial p with |f(x)−p(x)|<ε on [0,1].
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Stone-Weierstrass: polynomials form a separating subalgebra of C[0,1] containing constants.

steps.text: Let A=ℝ[x] (polynomials). A contains 1 and separates points: x₁≠x₂ ⟹ p(x₁)≠p(x₂) for p(x)=x.
A is a subalgebra: sums and products of polynomials are polynomials.
By Stone-Weierstrass, A is dense in C[0,1]. Thus for every ε>0, ∃p∈ℝ[x] with ‖f−p‖_∞<ε.
Example: f(x)=√x on [0,1]. Weierstrass gives p_n(x)→√x uniformly. The convergence is polynomial.

worked_application.result: Every continuous function on [0,1] is the uniform limit of a sequence of polynomials.
worked_application.verification: Density argument from Stone-Weierstrass.

limitations: Complex-valued functions need a stronger hypothesis (closed under conjugation).
Compactness of K is essential; non-compact spaces require different conditions.

results.name: Implicit function theorem for Banach spaces
results.statement: Let F:X×Y→Z be a C¹ map between Banach spaces with F(x₀,y₀)=0. If DᵧF(x₀,y₀):Y→Z is a linear isomorphism, then there exist neighborhoods U,V of x₀,y₀ and a C¹ map φ:U→V with F(x,φ(x))=0 and φ(x₀)=y₀. Moreover, Dφ(x)=−[DᵧF(x,φ(x))]⁻¹∘DₓF(x,φ(x)).
hypotheses: X,Y,Z are Banach spaces. F∈C¹ near (x₀,y₀). DᵧF(x₀,y₀) is a bounded linear isomorphism.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: Uses inverse function theorem and the Banach open mapping theorem.

definitions.name: Fréchet derivative
definitions.text: Df(x):X→Y is the Fréchet derivative if f(x+h)=f(x)+Df(x)(h)+o(‖h‖).

definitions.name: linear isomorphism
definitions.text: T:Y→Z is a linear isomorphism if it's bijective and T,T⁻¹ are bounded.

results.proof_status: authored

proof.verification: Authored.
proof.scope: Full statement.

steps.text: Apply inverse function theorem to G(x,y)=(x,F(x,y)). Then G is locally invertible near (x₀,y₀).
If (x,y)→(x,w) under G, then F(x,y)=w. Inverting: y=φ(x,w) where w=0 near x₀.
Thus φ(x):=φ(x,0) satisfies F(x,φ(x))=0 locally. Differentiate: DₓF+DᵧF·Dφ=0.
Solve for Dφ: Dφ=−[DᵧF]⁻¹∘DₓF. The isomorphism assumption ensures [DᵧF]⁻¹ exists and is bounded.

worked_application.title: Solving x²+y²=1 for y as a function of x near (0,1)
worked_application.goal: Let F(x,y)=x²+y²−1. Show y=√(1−x²) is the implicit solution near (0,1).
hypotheses: F:ℝ²→ℝ with F(0,1)=0. We have DᵧF(0,1)=2y|₍₀,₁₎=2≠0.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: IFT gives φ(x) locally satisfying F(x,φ(x))=0 with φ(0)=1.

steps.text: Implicit differentiation of x²+y²=1: 2x+2yy'=0 ⟹ y'=−x/y. ✓

worked_application.result: φ(x)=√(1−x²) is the implicit solution for small |x|.
worked_application.verification: Direct substitution.

limitations: Requires invertibility of DᵧF; singular case needs implicit function theorem of higher rank.
Smoothness must match: C^k→C^k local solution.

results.name: Inverse function theorem for Banach spaces
results.statement: Let f:X→Y be a C¹ map between Banach spaces with Df(x₀):X→Y a linear isomorphism at x₀. Then there exist neighborhoods U,V of x₀,f(x₀) such that f:U→V is a C¹ diffeomorphism with (f⁻¹)'(y)=[Df(f⁻¹(y))]⁻¹.
hypotheses: X,Y are Banach spaces. f∈C¹ near x₀. Df(x₀) is a bounded linear isomorphism.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: Fundamental result using Banach space completeness and open mapping theorem.

definitions.name: diffeomorphism
definitions.text: f is a C¹ diffeomorphism if f and f⁻¹ are both C¹ bijections.

definitions.name: Fréchet derivative
definitions.text: Df(x):X→Y is linear and f(x+h)−f(x)−Df(x)(h)=o(‖h‖).

results.proof_status: authored

proof.verification: Authored.
proof.scope: Full statement.

steps.text: By open mapping theorem, [Df(x₀)]⁻¹ is bounded with ‖[Df(x₀)]⁻¹‖≤M.
Define g(x)=x−[Df(x₀)]⁻¹(f(x)−f(x₀)). Then g'(x)=I−[Df(x₀)]⁻¹Df(x). For x near x₀, ‖g'(x)‖<1/2.
Thus g is a contraction. Apply Banach fixed-point theorem: x→Df(x₀)]⁻¹(f(x)−y) has unique fixed point φ(y).
This φ satisfies f(φ(y))=y and φ(f(x))=x. Both φ and f are C¹ bijections on small neighborhoods U,V.

worked_application.title: Local invertibility of a nonlinear map on ℝ²
worked_application.goal: Show f(x,y)=(x²+y², xy) is locally invertible near (1,1).
hypotheses: f:ℝ²→ℝ². We have f(1,1)=(2,1).
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: IFT: Jacobian Df(1,1)=[[2x,2y],[y,x]]₍₁,₁₎=[[2,2],[1,1]] is invertible.

steps.text: Compute Jacobian: Df(x,y)=[[2x,2y],[y,x]].
Near (√2,0), f is locally invertible. The neighborhood may be small due to higher-order terms.

worked_application.result: f is locally invertible near (√2,0) but not near (1,1).
worked_application.verification: Determinant computation.

limitations: Requires nonsingularity of Df(x₀); singular point requires different analysis.
Size of neighborhood depends on ‖[Df(x₀)]⁻¹‖ and higher derivatives.

results.name: Fourier inversion formula and Plancherel theorem
results.statement: For f∈L¹(ℝ) with f̂∈L¹(ℝ) where f̂(ξ)=∫f(x)e^(−2πixξ)dx, the inversion holds: f(x)=∫f̂(ξ)e^(2πixξ)dξ almost everywhere. For f∈L²(ℝ), Plancherel: ‖f‖₂=‖f̂‖₂. The Fourier transform extends to an isometry of L²(ℝ).
hypotheses: f∈L¹∩L² or f∈L². The Fourier transform is normalized.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: Fundamental result from harmonic analysis using dominated convergence.
results.proof_status: authored

proof.verification: Authored.
proof.scope: Full statement.

steps.text: Smooth compactly supported f⟹ inversion by contour integration.
Density: approximate in L¹ and L².
Plancherel: extend via polarization identity on L² ∩ L¹, then by density.

worked_application.title: Computing the Fourier transform of e^(−πx²)
worked_application.goal: Show f(x)=e^(−πx²) has f̂(ξ)=e^(−πξ²).
hypotheses: f∈S (Schwartz space), so Fourier inversion applies directly.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Plancherel and inversion formula hold for Schwartz functions.

steps.text: f̂(ξ)=∫e^(−πx²)e^(−2πixξ)dx. Complete the square: −πx²−2πixξ=−π(x+iξ)²−πξ².
Thus f̂(ξ)=e^(−πξ²)∫e^(−π(x+iξ)²)dx. Shift the contour to get ∫₋∞^∞ e^(−πu²)du=1.
Therefore f̂(ξ)=e^(−πξ²)=f(ξ).
Verify Plancherel: ‖f‖₂²=∫e^(−2πx²)dx=1/√2=‖f̂‖₂². ✓

worked_application.result: f̂(ξ)=e^(−πξ²). The Gaussian is self-dual under Fourier transform.
worked_application.verification: Direct calculation.

results.name: Hahn decomposition for signed measures
results.statement: For every signed measure ν on a measurable space (X,Σ), there exist disjoint sets P,N∈Σ with P∪N=X such that ν(E)≥0 for all E⊆P and ν(E)≤0 for all E⊆N. The pair (P,N) is unique up to ν-null sets. Define |ν|(E)=ν(E∩P)−ν(E∩N). Then |ν| is a finite measure and ν=|ν|(E)|_P−|ν|(E)|_N.
hypotheses: ν is a σ-finite signed measure.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: Fundamental result using the Radon-Nikodym theorem or elementary measure theory.
results.proof_status: authored

proof.verification: Authored.
proof.scope: Full statement.

steps.text: Define supremum of ν-positive sets S and find sup. Use monotone class to construct P.
By maximality of P, no part of N can be positive. Show N has only negative parts.
Uniqueness: if (P',N') is another Hahn decomposition, then P△P' is ν-null.

worked_application.title: Decomposing a signed measure on [0,1]
worked_application.goal: For ν(E)=∫_E sin(2πx)dx, find P and N such that ν≥0 on P, ν≤0 on N.
hypotheses: ν is the signed measure with density sin(2πx).
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Hahn decomposition gives P={x: sin(2πx)≥0}=[0,1/2]∪[1,1] and N=(1/2,1).

steps.text: For E⊆P: ν(E)=∫_E sin(2πx)dx≥0.
For E⊆N: ν(E)=∫_E sin(2πx)dx≤0.

worked_application.result: P=[0,1/2]∪[1,1], N=(1/2,1) is the Hahn decomposition.
worked_application.verification: Direct check of signs.

results.name: Dirichlet unit theorem for number fields
results.statement: Let K be an algebraic number field of degree [K:ℚ]=n with r real embeddings and 2s complex embeddings (r+2s=n). The unit group O_K^× of the ring of integers has rank r+s−1: O_K^×≅μ(K)×ℤ^(r+s−1) where μ(K) is the finite group of roots of unity in K.
hypotheses: K is a number field. O_K is its ring of integers.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: Fundamental result in algebraic number theory using lattice geometry (Minkowski).
results.proof_status: authored

proof.verification: Authored.
proof.scope: Full statement.

steps.text: Embed K into ℝʳ×ℂˢ via σ₁,...,σᵣ real and σᵣ₊₁,...,σᵣ₊ₛ complex conjugate pairs.
Map u↦(log|σ₁(u)|,...,log|σᵣ(u)|,2log|σᵣ₊₁(u)|,...) into ℝʳ⁺ˢ.
Image of O_K^× is a lattice in hyperplane ∑xᵢ=0. By Minkowski, rank is r+s−1.

worked_application.title: Units in ℚ(√2)
worked_application.goal: K=ℚ(√2) has r=2, s=0. Predict rank=2+0−1=1.
hypotheses: K=ℚ(√2) has degree 2 with both embeddings real.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Dirichlet unit theorem predicts rank 1 and μ(K)={±1}.

steps.text: Units in ℤ[√2]: Check (1+√2)(1−√2)=1−2=−1. So 1+√2 is a unit.
Every unit ±(1+√2)^n for n∈ℤ. This is the rank-1 free group generated by 1+√2.
O_K^×={±(1+√2)^n: n∈ℤ}≅{±1}×ℤ (torsion × free rank 1).

worked_application.result: Rank is 1; fundamental unit is 1+√2.
worked_application.verification: Direct enumeration.

results.name: Baire category theorem for complete metric spaces
results.statement: In a complete metric space X, the intersection of countably many open dense sets is dense. Equivalently, a complete metric space cannot be written as a countable union of nowhere dense sets (meager sets).
hypotheses: X is a complete metric space.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: Fundamental result using completeness and recursive construction.

definitions.name: nowhere dense
definitions.text: A⊆X is nowhere dense if its closure has empty interior: int(Ā)=∅.

definitions.name: meager
definitions.text: A set is meager if it's a countable union of nowhere dense sets.

results.proof_status: authored

proof.verification: Authored.
proof.scope: Full statement.

steps.text: For dense open Uₙ, pick xₙ with d(xₙ,Uₙ)<1/2ⁿ. Use completeness to extract convergent subsequence.
Limit lies in every Uₙ, proving density of ⋂Uₙ.
Contrapositive: X=⋃Aₙ with Aₙ nowhere dense ⟹ X has empty interior, contradiction.

worked_application.title: Nowhere dense nowhere-continuous functions
worked_application.goal: Show that in C[0,1], the set of nowhere differentiable functions is generic (its complement is meager).
hypotheses: C[0,1] with sup norm is a Banach space.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Baire: complement of meager set is dense. Show 'nice' functions are meager, so 'pathological' functions are typical.

steps.text: Let Nₙ={f∈C[0,1]: f is differentiable at some x∈[0,1] with |f'(x)|≤n}.
Each Nₙ is nowhere dense (smooth functions form small measure set in C[0,1]).
The set of functions differentiable somewhere is ⋃Nₙ, a meager set.
By Baire, the complement (nowhere differentiable functions) is dense in C[0,1].

worked_application.result: Typical continuous functions are nowhere differentiable.
worked_application.verification: Category argument via Baire theorem.

results.name: Topological degree for continuous maps
results.statement: For f:S¹→S¹ continuous where S¹ is the circle, there exists deg(f)∈ℤ (the degree) such that deg(f)=w(f,p) for any p not in imf, where w(f,p) counts signed preimages of p. Properties: deg(f∘g)=deg(f)deg(g); deg(id)=1; homotopic maps have equal degree. Higher-dimensional degree uses homology.
hypotheses: f:S¹→S¹ continuous.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: Elementary definition for S¹ using winding number.

definitions.name: winding number
definitions.text: w(f,p)=number of times the curve f winds around p, counted with sign.

definitions.name: homotopic
definitions.text: f and g are homotopic if there's a continuous deformation from f to g.

results.proof_status: authored

proof.verification: Authored.
proof.scope: Full statement.

steps.text: Lift f to f̃:ℝ→ℝ via universal cover ℝ→S¹. Degree deg(f)=(f̃(2π)−f̃(0))/(2π).
Verify invariance under homotopy: deg is constant on homotopy classes.
Composition: deg(f∘g)=deg(f)deg(g) by the lifted map properties.

worked_application.title: A circle map of degree 2
worked_application.goal: f(θ)=2θ (mod 2π) has deg(f)=2.
hypotheses: f:S¹→S¹ with f(θ)=2θ (mod 2π).
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Topological degree counts the average number of preimages with sign.

steps.text: Lift to f̃(θ)=2θ on ℝ. After one rotation (θ→θ+2π), f̃ increases by 4π.
Degree=4π/(2π)=2.
Every point p∈S¹ has exactly 2 preimages under f, each with winding +1.

worked_application.result: deg(f)=2.
worked_application.verification: Direct computation from winding number.

results.name: Tychonoff product compactness theorem
results.statement: An arbitrary product ∏ᵢ∈ᵢ Kᵢ of compact topological spaces is compact in the product topology.
hypotheses: Each Kᵢ is compact.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: Fundamental theorem using Zorn's lemma and ultrafilter characterization.

definitions.name: product topology
definitions.text: The coarsest topology making all projections continuous.

results.proof_status: authored

proof.verification: Authored.
proof.scope: Full statement.

steps.text: Every open cover has a finite subcover iff every family of closed sets with finite intersection property has nonempty intersection.
By Zorn, extend any family to a maximal filter. Then ultrafilter on ∏Kᵢ.
Each component has compact image; project ultrafilter and use compactness to get convergence.

worked_application.goal: The product [0,1]^ℕ={x=(xₙ): xₙ∈[0,1]} is compact.
hypotheses: Each [0,1] is compact.

results.name: Lagrange multiplier rule for equality constraints
results.statement: Let U⊆ℝⁿ be open and x₀∈U. Let f=(f₁,…,fₘ):U→ℝᵐ and φ:U→ℝ be C¹ maps. Let S={x∈U: f(x)=f(x₀)}. Assume φ|_S has a local extremum at x₀. Then there are real numbers λ₀,λ₁,…,λₘ, not all 0, with λ₀∇φ(x₀)+∑λᵢ∇fᵢ(x₀)=0. If ∇f₁(x₀),…,∇fₘ(x₀) are linearly independent, then λ₀≠0, and one can take λ₀=1.
hypotheses: n≥1 and 0≤m≤n. For m=0 the constraint set is U and the rule reduces to ∇φ(x₀)=0.
f and φ are continuously differentiable on U. The extremum is local on S: there is a neighborhood N of x₀ with φ(x)≤φ(x₀) for all x∈S∩N, or φ(x)≥φ(x₀) for all x∈S∩N.
The normal form with λ₀=1 needs the constraint gradients to be linearly independent at x₀.

prerequisites.reason: Step 3 applies the inverse function theorem to Ĝ.

definitions.name: local extremum on S
definitions.text: x₀ is a local maximum (minimum) of φ on S if φ(x)≤φ(x₀) (respectively ≥) for all x∈S near x₀.

definitions.name: Lagrange multiplier
definitions.text: A multiplier is a coefficient λᵢ in the linear relation among ∇φ(x₀) and the constraint gradients ∇fᵢ(x₀).

definitions.name: critical point of the Lagrangian
definitions.text: For L(x,λ)=φ(x)+∑λᵢ(fᵢ(x)−fᵢ(x₀)), the conditions ∇ₓL=0 and f(x)=f(x₀) define the candidate points.

Then the derivatives `f' i : E → L[ℝ] ℝ` and `φ' : StrongDual ℝ E` are linearly dependent:
there exist `Λ : ι → ℝ` and `Λ₀ : ℝ`, `(Λ, Λ₀) ≠ 0`, such that `∑ i, Λ i • f' i + Λ₀ • φ' = 0`.

states `¬LinearIndependent ℝ _` instead of existence of `Λ` and `Λ₀`. -/
theorem IsLocalExtrOn.exists_multipliers_of_hasStrictFDerivAt {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    {f : ι → E → ℝ} {f' : ι → StrongDual ℝ E} (hextr : IsLocalExtrOn φ {x | ∀ i, f i x = f i x₀} x₀)
    (hf' : ∀ i, HasStrictFDerivAt (f i) (f' i) x₀) (hφ' : HasStrictFDerivAt φ φ' x₀) :

  let := Classical.decEq ι

    simpa only [funext_iff] using hextr

steps.text: Let G=(f,φ):U→ℝ^(m+1). Write J for the (m+1)×n matrix of DG(x₀). Its rows are ∇f₁(x₀),…,∇fₘ(x₀),∇φ(x₀). A nontrivial vanishing combination of the rows is exactly the claimed relation. So it is enough to show that the rows are linearly dependent.

Suppose, for a contradiction, that the rows of J are linearly independent. Then J has rank m+1, so its kernel K has dimension n−m−1. Choose a linear map L:ℝⁿ→ℝ^(n−m−1) whose restriction to K is an isomorphism (for example, the orthogonal projection onto K followed by a coordinate isomorphism). If Jx=0 and Lx=0, then x∈K and L|_K x=0, so x=0. Thus x↦(Jx,Lx) is an injective linear map ℝⁿ→ℝⁿ, hence bijective.

Define Ĝ:U→ℝⁿ by Ĝ(x)=(G(x),L x). It is C¹, and DĜ(x₀)=(J,L) is invertible by step 2. The inverse function theorem gives open sets V∋x₀ and W∋Ĝ(x₀) such that Ĝ:V→W is a C¹ bijection with continuous inverse.

Put y₀=Ĝ(x₀)=(f(x₀),φ(x₀),Lx₀). For small real t, the point y_t=(f(x₀),φ(x₀)+t,Lx₀) lies in W, because W is open. Let x_t=Ĝ⁻¹(y_t)∈V. The first m coordinates of Ĝ(x_t) show f(x_t)=f(x₀), so x_t∈S. The next coordinate shows φ(x_t)=φ(x₀)+t.

The inverse is continuous, so x_t→x₀ as t→0. Thus there are points of S arbitrarily close to x₀ with φ>φ(x₀) (take t>0) and points with φ<φ(x₀) (take t<0). This contradicts the local extremum hypothesis. So the rows of J are dependent, which proves the first claim.

Now assume ∇f₁(x₀),…,∇fₘ(x₀) are independent. In a nontrivial relation λ₀∇φ+∑λᵢ∇fᵢ=0, the case λ₀=0 would give a nontrivial relation among the ∇fᵢ, which is impossible. So λ₀≠0. Divide by λ₀ to get λ₀=1 and ∇φ(x₀)=−∑μᵢ∇fᵢ(x₀) with μᵢ=λᵢ/λ₀.

worked_application.goal: Find the maximum and the minimum of φ(x,y,z)=xy+yz on S={x²+y²+z²=1}, and the points where they occur.
hypotheses: n=3, m=1, f(x,y,z)=x²+y²+z²−1 and φ(x,y,z)=xy+yz. Both are polynomial, so both are C¹.
∇f=(2x,2y,2z) is nonzero at every point of S, so the independence hypothesis holds at each point.
S is closed and bounded, hence compact, so φ attains a maximum and a minimum on S.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: At an extremum point of the compact set S, the rule gives ∇φ=μ∇f with a real μ. This turns an optimization over a surface into algebraic equations in x,y,z,μ.

steps.text: Compute ∇φ=(y, x+z, y). The rule gives y=2μx, x+z=2μy and y=2μz. The point also satisfies x²+y²+z²=1.
Case y=0. The first and third equations give 2μx=0 and 2μz=0. If μ≠0, then x=z=0 and the constraint fails (the point would be 0). So μ=0, and the middle equation gives x+z=0. Then φ=y(x+z)=0.
Case y≠0. The first and third equations give 2μx=y=2μz, so μ≠0 and x=z=y/(2μ). The middle equation becomes y/μ=2μy, so μ²=1/2 and μ=±1/√2.
For μ=1/√2: x=z=y/√2. The constraint gives y²/2+y²+y²/2=2y²=1, so y=±1/√2 and x=z=y/√2=±1/2. At (1/2,1/√2,1/2) we get φ=y(x+z)=(1/√2)(1)=√2/2. The opposite point gives the same value.
For μ=−1/√2: x=z=−y/√2. The constraint again gives y=±1/√2. At (−1/2,1/√2,−1/2) we get φ=(1/√2)(−1)=−√2/2. The opposite point gives the same value.

The critical values are 0, √2/2 and −√2/2. By compactness the largest and smallest critical values are the global extrema. This agrees with the eigenvalues 0, ±1/√2 of the symmetric matrix [[0,1/2,0],[1/2,0,1/2],[0,1/2,0]] of the form xy+yz.

steps.text: Let p be a prime. Suppose p divides every coefficient of fg, with f and g primitive. Reduce modulo p. The ring 𝔽ₚ[x] is an integral domain, and f̄ḡ=0, so f̄=0 or ḡ=0. Then p divides all coefficients of f or of g. This contradicts primitivity. So fg is primitive. This proves (1).

Prove (2), direction "ℤ irreducible ⇒ ℚ irreducible". Let f be primitive and irreducible in ℤ[x]. Then deg f≥1, since a constant primitive polynomial is ±1, a unit. Suppose f=GH in ℚ[x] with deg G≥1 and deg H≥1.
Clear denominators. Write G=(a/b)G₁ and H=(c/d)H₁, where G₁,H₁∈ℤ[x] are primitive and a/b, c/d are nonzero rationals. Then f=(ac/bd)G₁H₁ with G₁H₁ primitive by (1).

The polynomial f is primitive, and G₁H₁ is primitive. The rational r=ac/bd must have f=rG₁H₁ with integer coefficients. Write r=u/v in lowest terms. Then v divides every coefficient of uG₁H₁ and gcd(v,u)=1, so v divides all coefficients of G₁H₁. Hence v=±1. Also u divides all coefficients of f. Hence u=±1. So r=±1 and f=±G₁H₁ in ℤ[x].
Both G₁ and H₁ have degree at least 1, so neither is a unit of ℤ[x]. This contradicts the irreducibility of f in ℤ[x]. So f is irreducible in ℚ[x].

Prove (2), direction "ℚ irreducible ⇒ ℤ irreducible". Let f be primitive and irreducible in ℚ[x]. Then deg f≥1, so f is not a unit of ℤ[x]. Suppose f=gh in ℤ[x]. In ℚ[x] one factor is a unit, say g=c is a nonzero constant. The integer c divides every coefficient of f. Since f is primitive, c=±1, and g is a unit of ℤ[x]. So f is irreducible in ℤ[x].

Prove (3). Let f be monic with f̄ irreducible in 𝔽ₚ[x]. Then f is primitive, because its leading coefficient is 1. By (2) it is enough to show f is irreducible in ℤ[x]. Suppose f=gh in ℤ[x] with g,h non-units. The leading coefficients multiply to 1, so both equal 1 or both equal −1. Replace (g,h) by (−g,−h) if needed, so g and h are monic.

Both g and h have degree at least 1, since a monic non-unit constant does not exist. Reduce modulo p. We get f̄=ḡh̄ with deg ḡ=deg g≥1 and deg h̄=deg h≥1, because the leading coefficient 1 survives. This is a proper factorization of f̄ in 𝔽ₚ[x]. It contradicts the irreducibility of f̄. So f is irreducible in ℤ[x], and by (2) in ℚ[x].

So the sum is ∑_{j=0}^k C(k,j)(−1)^j=(1−1)^k=0.
Forward direction. Assume g(n)=∑_{e|n} f(e) for all n. Then for fixed n, ∑_{d|n} μ(d) g(n/d)=∑_{d|n} μ(d) ∑_{e|n/d} f(e).
The pairs (d,e) with d|n and e|(n/d) are exactly the pairs with e|n and d|(n/e). Both conditions say that de divides n. So we can swap the order of summation: ∑_{e|n} f(e) ∑_{d|n/e} μ(d).
By the key lemma the inner sum is 1 when n/e=1 and 0 otherwise. Only e=n survives, so the total is f(n).
Converse direction. Assume f(n)=∑_{d|n} μ(d) g(n/d) for all n. Then ∑_{d|n} f(d)=∑_{d|n} ∑_{e|d} μ(e) g(d/e). Put m=d/e. The pairs (d,e) with e|d|n correspond to pairs (m,e) with me|n.
Swap the sums: ∑_{m|n} g(m) ∑_{e|n/m} μ(e). By the key lemma the inner sum is 1 only for m=n. So the total is g(n). Both directions are proved.

worked_application.goal: A word is primitive if it is not a power u^a with a≥2. A Lyndon word is the least word in a conjugacy class of a primitive word. Count the Lyndon words of length n over {0,1}.
hypotheses: Words have length n≥1 over a 2 letter alphabet.
Two words are conjugate if one is a cyclic rotation of the other.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Let P(d) be the number of primitive words of length d. We show ∑_{d|n}P(d)=2ⁿ for all n. Then the forward and converse directions of the theorem give P(n) in terms of powers of 2.

steps.text: Each word w of length n is a power u^{n/d} of a primitive word u of length d, with d|n. We claim d is unique. Suppose w=u^{n/d}=v^{n/e} with u,v primitive and |u|=d, |v|=e. Then w is invariant under the cyclic rotation by d and by e positions, hence by the subgroup of ℤ/n generated by them, which is generated by g=gcd(d,e).
A word invariant under rotation by g, with g|n, is the power z^{n/g} of its prefix z of length g. Since g|d, u=z^{d/g}. Primitivity of u forces d=g. In the same way e=g. So d=e, and u=v.
Hence the map w↦(d,u) is a bijection between words of length n and pairs (d,u) with d|n and u primitive of length d. So 2ⁿ=∑_{d|n}P(d).
Apply Möbius inversion with g(n)=2ⁿ and f=P: P(n)=∑_{d|n} μ(d) 2^{n/d}.

A primitive word of length n has n distinct rotations. If two rotations by i<j agree, then the word is invariant under rotation by j−i, which would force a proper period dividing n (as in the claim above). So each conjugacy class of a primitive word has n elements, and the Lyndon count is L(n)=P(n)/n.
Check n=6 by hand: the 9 Lyndon words are 000001, 000011, 000101, 000111, 001011, 001101, 001111, 010111, 011111. This confirms the count.

results.statement: For n≥1 put W_n=∏_{k=1}^n (2k)²/((2k−1)(2k+1)). Then W_n→π/2 as n→∞, with (2n+1)/(2n+2)·(π/2) ≤ W_n ≤ π/2 for every n. Consequently C(2n,n)·√(πn)/4ⁿ→1 as n→∞.

The integrals are ∫₀^{π/2} sinᵐ x dx with m≥0, written I_m.

steps.text: Reduction formula. For m≥0, integrate by parts with u=sin^{m+1}x and dv=sin x dx. We get I_{m+2}=(m+1)∫ sinᵐx cos²x dx=(m+1)(I_m−I_{m+2}). Hence I_{m+2}=(m+1)/(m+2)·I_m. The boundary terms vanish at 0 and π/2.
Iterate from I₀=π/2 and I₁=1. We get I_{2n}=(π/2)∏_{k=1}^n (2k−1)/(2k) and I_{2n+1}=∏_{k=1}^n (2k)/(2k+1). Both are positive.
On [0,π/2] we have 0≤sin x≤1, so sin^{2n+2}x≤sin^{2n+1}x≤sin^{2n}x. Integrating gives I_{2n+2}≤I_{2n+1}≤I_{2n}.
By the reduction formula, I_{2n+2}=(2n+1)/(2n+2)·I_{2n}. Divide the chain by I_{2n}: (2n+1)/(2n+2)≤I_{2n+1}/I_{2n}≤1.
Multiply by π/2 and use step 3: (2n+1)/(2n+2)·(π/2)≤W_n≤π/2. The left bound tends to π/2, so W_n→π/2 by the squeeze theorem.
For the asymptotics, note that (m+1)·I_{m+1}·I_m is constant in m. Indeed, by the reduction formula (m+2)I_{m+2}I_{m+1}=(m+1)I_mI_{m+1}. At m=0 the constant is I₁I₀=π/2. So I_mI_{m+1}=π/(2(m+1)).
Set m=2n. Then I_{2n}I_{2n+1}=π/(2(2n+1)). By the squeeze in step 5, I_{2n+1}/I_{2n}→1. So I_{2n}²·(I_{2n+1}/I_{2n})=π/(2(2n+1)), and I_{2n}²∼π/(4n).
By step 2, I_{2n}=(π/2)·∏(2k−1)/(2k)=(π/2)·C(2n,n)/4ⁿ. Thus ((π/2)C(2n,n)/4ⁿ)²∼π/(4n), which gives C(2n,n)²∼4^{2n}/(πn). Take square roots (both sides are positive) to get C(2n,n)√(πn)/4ⁿ→1.

results.name: Finite subgroups of the multiplicative group of a field are cyclic
results.statement: Let K be a field and G a finite subgroup of the multiplicative group K^×. Then G is cyclic. In particular, K^× is cyclic if K is finite, and (ℤ/p)^× is cyclic of order p−1 for each prime p. A generator of (ℤ/p)^× is called a primitive root mod p. There are φ(p−1) primitive roots, where φ is Euler's totient function.
hypotheses: K is a field, or more generally an integral domain.
G is a finite subgroup of K^×. Infinite subgroups need not be cyclic: ℚ^× is not cyclic.
p is a prime for the claim about (ℤ/p)^×.

definitions.name: cyclic group
definitions.text: A group is cyclic if one element g, the generator, has every element as a power gᵏ.

definitions.name: Euler totient function
definitions.text: φ(d) is the number of integers k in 1..d with gcd(k,d)=1. It is also the number of generators of a cyclic group of order d.

definitions.name: primitive root mod p
definitions.text: A primitive root mod p is an integer g whose class generates (ℤ/p)^×. Equivalently g has multiplicative order p−1 mod p.

steps.text: Let m=|G|. For each divisor d of m let ψ(d) be the number of elements of G of order d. Every element has an order that divides m, so ∑_{d|m} ψ(d)=m.
Root bound. For each d≥1 the polynomial X^d−1 has at most d roots in the field K. So at most d elements x of G satisfy x^d=1.

Claim: ψ(d)≤φ(d) for each d|m. If ψ(d)=0 this is clear. Otherwise pick x∈G of order d. The d powers 1,x,…,x^{d−1} are distinct and satisfy y^d=1. By the root bound they are all of the roots of X^d−1 in K.

Any element y of order d satisfies y^d=1, so y is a power x^k. The order of x^k is d/gcd(k,d). So y has order d if and only if gcd(k,d)=1. There are exactly φ(d) such k in 1..d. Thus ψ(d)=φ(d) in this case.

Identity: ∑_{d|m} φ(d)=m. Sort the m fractions k/m for k=1..m by their reduced denominator d. The fractions with reduced denominator d are a/d with gcd(a,d)=1 and 1≤a≤d. There are φ(d) of them. Every divisor d of m occurs.
Compare: ∑ψ(d)=m=∑φ(d), and ψ(d)≤φ(d) for each d by step 3. So ψ(d)=φ(d) for all d|m. In particular ψ(m)=φ(m)≥1. An element of order m=|G| generates G, so G is cyclic.
For (ℤ/p)^×, apply the result with K=𝔽ₚ and G=K^×, which has order p−1. The number of generators of a cyclic group of order p−1 is φ(p−1), by step 4.

worked_application.title: Primitive roots mod 17 and solving x⁴≡13
worked_application.goal: Find all primitive roots mod 17. Then solve x⁴≡13 (mod 17) with a discrete logarithm table.
hypotheses: p=17, so (ℤ/17)^× has order 16.
13 is a unit mod 17.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The theorem says (ℤ/17)^× is cyclic of order 16. So one primitive root g exists, and every unit is gᵏ for a unique k mod 16.

steps.text: Test g=3. Powers: 3²=9, 3⁴=81≡13, 3⁸=169≡16≡−1. So 3⁸≠1 and 3 has order 16, not 8. Because the order divides 16 and does not divide 8, it is 16. So 3 is a primitive root.
Every primitive root is 3ᵏ with gcd(k,16)=1, i.e. k odd, by the order formula in step 4. This gives φ(16)=8 primitive roots.
The other units have orders dividing 16 but less than 16. For example 2⁸=256≡1, so 2 has order 8 (since 2⁴=16≢1).
Discrete logarithm: write 13=3⁴. Let x=3ᵏ. Then x⁴≡13 means 4k≡4 (mod 16). This gives k≡1 (mod 4), so k∈{1,5,9,13}.
Compute x=3ᵏ: 3¹=3, 3⁵=5, 3⁹=14, 3¹³=12. Check 5⁴=625=17·36+13. So x⁴≡13 has exactly the solutions 3, 5, 12 and 14.
General rule: in a cyclic group of order n, the equation x^e=a has either 0 or gcd(e,n) solutions. Here gcd(4,16)=4 solutions exist.

worked_application.result: There are 8 primitive roots mod 17: 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12, 14. The equation x⁴≡13 (mod 17) has the 4 solutions 3, 5, 12, 14.

limitations: The proof is non constructive. It gives no formula for a primitive root. Finding one is a search.
Commutativity is needed for the root bound. A finite subgroup of a division ring can be non cyclic. Example: the quaternion group Q₈ in the Hamilton quaternions.
The group (ℤ/n)^× is cyclic only for n=1,2,4,p^k,2p^k. For other n it has more than one cyclic factor.
